_comment: The drone's camera rig, as hardware. Every number here is a measurement
or a stand-in for one -- nothing in delta/rig.py hard-codes a camera.
Ported from the glasses project. Same baseboard, same sensors, different
mounting: these two lenses sit inside a 30 cm sphere on a gimbal that
keeps them level while the shell rolls.
Frame: the sensor head's own frame. Origin at the centre of the sphere,
+x right, +y up, -z forward. Habitat's convention.
yaw is degrees, POSITIVE IS LEFT.
pitch is degrees, POSITIVE IS DOWN.
hfov is HORIZONTAL degrees; pixels are square, so fx == fy.

hardware.sensor: AR0234, colour global shutter, 1920x1200, M12 mount
hardware.lens: PENDING -- M12, target ~120 HFOV, not the stock lens
hardware.gimbal: PENDING -- 2-axis, holds the pair level as the shell rolls

_comment: What stereo actually runs on. Deliberately separate from capture:
SGBM cost scales with pixels x disparity range.

baseline_status: ASSUMED. Reduced from the glasses' 12 cm: the whole drone is 30 cm
across, and the pair has to fit inside it with gimbal clearance.
The cost is real and worth knowing -- depth error grows as the
baseline shrinks, so 8 cm is about 1.5x the range error of 12 cm at
the same distance. Measure centre-to-centre once the frame is printed.
measured.hfov_status: TARGET -- measure what the lens actually gives
pitch_status: LEVEL, and it has to stay level in V1.
Tilting the cameras down is tempting for a robot 15 cm off the floor,
and it was tried: 12 degrees measured the camera height as 0.07 m
The reason is stereo.estimate_floor. It finds the floor as a spike in a
histogram of point height, which only works while every floor point has
the same height in camera coordinates -- that is, while the camera is
level. Tilt it and a flat floor becomes a slope in those coordinates,
the spike smears, and the lowest surviving bin is somewhere up the
slope rather than the floor itself.
A tilt is still worth having later, because more floor pixels make a
better map. It needs the points rotated into a level frame by this
known angle first, in BOTH estimate_floor and GapMap._place, and the
tracker pose levelled with them since the map frame is the first
camera frame. Do not simply raise this number.
Level costs little here because the lens is wide: at 120 degrees the
bottom of the frame points 47 degrees down, so a camera 16 cm up still
sees floor from about 15 cm ahead. Check with rig.ground_horizon().

cameras.name: left
cameras._comment: x is in BASELINES: -0.5 and +0.5 are one baseline apart.

_comment: The down-facing distance sensor under the inner frame: how far below
it the nearest surface is -- the floor, or a table the drone is
flying over. The brain's altitude comes from it (delta/brain/height.py).
Modelled on the HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor in the parts list: 2 cm to
4 m, a cone about 15 degrees wide that answers with the NEAREST echo
in it, and about half a centimetre of noise. A VL53L1X laser ToF would
be the same numbers with a narrower cone.
below_lens: how far under the lenses (the sphere's centre) it sits.
On the ground it is then 5 cm above the floor -- inside the 2 cm
minimum. PENDING: measure once the inner frame is printed.
OpenCV plumb-bob, [k1 k2 p1 p2 k3]. All zero == a perfect pinhole,
which is exactly what Habitat renders. The undistort stage runs anyway,
so that real checkerboard coefficients change this file and nothing else.
A rear-facing pair, if it happens. A drone that maps by exploring
spends half its time reversing out of rooms. Move these into
'cameras' to enable them.
